name: Hydrogen (H2)

dry_test.procedure: Hold a lit splint at the open end of a test tube.
dry_test.result: The gas burns with a characteristic 'squeaky pop' sound.

notes: Highly flammable. The pop is a miniature explosion of hydrogen mixing with oxygen.

name: Oxygen (O2)

dry_test.procedure: Insert a glowing splint into the test tube.
dry_test.result: The splint relights and bursts back into flame.

notes: Oxygen supports combustion.

name: Carbon Dioxide (CO2)

dry_test.procedure: Hold a lit splint in the gas.

wet_test.procedure: Bubble the gas through limewater (aqueous Calcium Hydroxide).
wet_test.result: The limewater turns milky/cloudy.

notes: The cloudiness is a fine precipitate of insoluble Calcium Carbonate (CaCO3).

name: Chlorine (Cl2)

dry_test.procedure: Hold damp blue litmus paper in the gas.
dry_test.result: The paper turns red (acidic) and is instantly bleached white.

wet_test.procedure: Pass through aqueous Potassium Iodide (KI).
wet_test.result: The colorless KI solution turns brown.

notes: Chlorine displaces iodine from KI. Highly toxic; always test in a fume hood.

name: Ammonia (NH3)

dry_test.procedure: Hold damp red litmus paper in the gas.

wet_test.procedure: Hold a glass rod dipped in concentrated Hydrochloric Acid (HCl) near the gas.
wet_test.result: Dense white fumes are produced.

notes: Ammonia is the only common alkaline gas. The fumes are solid Ammonium Chloride.

name: Nitrate Ion (NO3-)

dry_test.result: May evolve heavy, toxic brown fumes of Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2).

wet_test.procedure: Brown Ring Test: Add freshly prepared Iron(II) Sulfate (FeSO4) solution, then carefully pour concentrated Sulfuric Acid (H2SO4) down the side of the test tube.
wet_test.result: A distinct brown ring forms at the junction of the two liquids.

notes: The brown ring is a complex ion called pentaaquanitrosyliron(II).

name: Sulfate Ion (SO4 2-)

wet_test.procedure: Add dilute Hydrochloric acid (to remove carbonate impurities), followed by aqueous Barium Chloride (BaCl2).
wet_test.result: A dense white precipitate forms.

notes: Barium sulfate is highly insoluble, even in acidic conditions.

name: Chloride Ion (Cl-)

dry_test.procedure: Add concentrated Sulfuric Acid to the solid salt.
dry_test.result: Evolves steamy, acidic white fumes of Hydrogen Chloride (HCl).

wet_test.procedure: Add dilute Nitric acid (to remove impurities), followed by aqueous Silver Nitrate (AgNO3).
wet_test.result: A white precipitate forms which dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia.

notes: Silver chloride turns purple/grey upon exposure to sunlight due to photodecomposition.

name: Carbonate Ion (CO3 2-)

wet_test.procedure: Add any dilute acid (e.g., HCl or HNO3) to the solid or solution.
wet_test.result: Brisk effervescence (fizzing) as a colorless gas is evolved. The gas turns limewater milky.

notes: Confirms presence of carbonate or bicarbonate.

name: Copper(II) Ion (Cu 2+)

dry_test.procedure: Flame Test: Dip a nichrome wire in concentrated HCl, then in the salt, and hold in a roaring Bunsen flame.

wet_test.procedure: Add aqueous Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH) dropwise.
wet_test.result: A pale blue precipitate forms which is insoluble in excess NaOH.

notes: Adding excess aqueous Ammonia instead will dissolve the precipitate into a deep royal blue solution.

name: Iron(III) Ion (Fe 3+)

wet_test.procedure: Add aqueous Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH) dropwise.
wet_test.result: A rusty red-brown precipitate forms which is insoluble in excess.

notes: Unlike Iron(II) which forms a green precipitate, Iron(III) forms a distinctly brown solid.

name: Sulfur Dioxide (SO2)

dry_test.procedure: Hold damp blue litmus paper in the gas.
dry_test.result: The paper turns red (acidic) and is then bleached white.

wet_test.procedure: Bubble the gas through acidified potassium dichromate solution (K2Cr2O7 + H2SO4).
wet_test.result: The orange solution turns green.
wet_test.equation: SO2 + K2Cr2O7 + H2SO4 -> K2SO4 + Cr2(SO4)3 + H2O

notes: SO2 acts as a reducing agent, reducing Cr(VI) to Cr(III). Highly toxic; use a fume hood.

name: Hydrogen Sulfide (H2S)

dry_test.procedure: Hold lead acetate paper in the gas.
dry_test.result: The paper turns black or brown.

wet_test.procedure: Pass the gas through cadmium nitrate or lead acetate solution.
wet_test.result: A yellow or black precipitate forms.

notes: Identified by its characteristic rotten egg smell. Highly toxic; always test in a fume hood.

name: Nitric Oxide (NO)

dry_test.procedure: Expose the colorless gas to air.
dry_test.result: The gas immediately turns brown as it reacts with oxygen to form Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2).

notes: NO is a neutral oxide and is paramagnetic. The brown color change on contact with air is the key identification feature.

name: Water Vapor (H2O)

dry_test.procedure: Hold anhydrous copper(II) sulfate (white powder) in the gas.

notes: Confirms the presence of water vapor. Equation: CuSO4 + 5H2O -> CuSO4.5H2O. Anhydrous CuSO4 is a reliable test for water.

name: Sulfite Ion (SO3 2-)

wet_test.procedure: Add aqueous Barium Chloride (BaCl2) solution. A white precipitate forms. Then add dilute Hydrochloric Acid (HCl).
wet_test.result: The white precipitate dissolves with effervescence (SO2 gas is evolved).
wet_test.equation: SO3 2- + Ba2+ -> BaSO3; BaSO3 + 2H+ -> Ba2+ + H2O + SO2

notes: This distinguishes sulfite from sulfate: BaSO4 does NOT dissolve in dilute acid, whereas BaSO3 does.

name: Phosphate Ion (PO4 3-)

wet_test.procedure: Add ammonium molybdate reagent [(NH4)2MoO4] and concentrated Nitric Acid (HNO3), then warm gently.
wet_test.result: A canary-yellow precipitate forms.

notes: A distinctive and specific test that does not work with other common anions. The yellow precipitate is ammonium phosphomolybdate.

name: Hydroxide Ion (OH-)

wet_test.procedure: Add a few drops of phenolphthalein indicator to the solution.
wet_test.result: The solution turns pink or magenta.

notes: Indicates an alkaline solution. Phenolphthalein is colorless in acidic and neutral solutions but turns pink above pH ~8.2.

name: Iodide Ion (I-)

dry_test.procedure: Add concentrated Sulfuric Acid (H2SO4) to the solid salt.
dry_test.result: Violet fumes of iodine (I2) are produced, along with a smell of rotten cabbage.

wet_test.procedure: Add dilute Nitric Acid (to remove impurities), followed by aqueous Silver Nitrate (AgNO3).
wet_test.result: A yellow precipitate (AgI) forms which is insoluble in dilute aqueous ammonia.

notes: Distinguishes from Cl- (white ppt, soluble in dilute NH3) and Br- (cream ppt, partially soluble in concentrated NH3).

name: Bromide Ion (Br-)

dry_test.procedure: Add concentrated Sulfuric Acid (H2SO4) to the solid salt.
dry_test.result: Reddish-brown fumes of bromine (Br2) are produced.

wet_test.procedure: Add dilute Nitric Acid (to remove impurities), followed by aqueous Silver Nitrate (AgNO3).
wet_test.result: A cream-colored precipitate (AgBr) forms which partially dissolves in concentrated aqueous ammonia.

notes: Intermediate behavior between Cl- and I- in terms of precipitate color and ammonia solubility.

name: Acetate Ion (CH3COO-)

wet_test.procedure: Add ethanol (C2H5OH) and concentrated Sulfuric Acid (H2SO4), then warm gently.
wet_test.result: A fruity, sweet smell of ethyl acetate ester is produced.

notes: Esterification test. The distinctive fruity odor of ethyl acetate confirms the presence of the acetate ion.

name: Sulfite Reducing Test (SO3 2-)

wet_test.procedure: Add acidified Potassium Permanganate (KMnO4) solution.
wet_test.result: The purple color of the permanganate is decolorized.

notes: Confirms the reducing nature of sulfite. SO3 2- is oxidized to SO4 2- while MnO4- is reduced from Mn(VII) to Mn(II).

name: Nitrite Ion (NO2-)

dry_test.procedure: Heat the solid salt with dilute Sulfuric Acid (H2SO4).
dry_test.result: Brown fumes of Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2) are evolved.

wet_test.procedure: Brown ring test variant: Add Iron(II) Sulfate (FeSO4) solution and acetic acid (CH3COOH) instead of concentrated H2SO4.
wet_test.result: A brown ring forms at the junction of the two liquids.

notes: Distinguishes from nitrate: nitrite gives the brown ring with weak acid (acetic acid), whereas nitrate requires concentrated H2SO4.

name: Zinc Ion (Zn2+)

wet_test.procedure: Add aqueous Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH) dropwise, then add excess NaOH.
wet_test.result: A white gelatinous precipitate forms initially, which dissolves in excess NaOH.

notes: Amphoteric behavior distinguishes Zn2+ from most other cations whose hydroxide precipitates do not dissolve in excess NaOH.

name: Calcium Ion (Ca2+)

dry_test.procedure: Flame Test: Dip a nichrome wire in concentrated HCl, then in the salt, and hold in a roaring Bunsen flame.
dry_test.result: Produces a brick red / orange-red flame.

wet_test.procedure: Add aqueous Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH) solution.
wet_test.result: No precipitate forms (or at most a very slight milky appearance).

notes: Calcium hydroxide is sparingly soluble, so no visible precipitate forms. The flame test is the definitive identification.

name: Lead(II) Ion (Pb2+)

wet_test.procedure: Add dilute Hydrochloric Acid (HCl) to form a white precipitate. Alternatively, add Potassium Iodide (KI) solution to form a bright yellow precipitate.
wet_test.result: With HCl: white precipitate of PbCl2 (soluble in hot water, re-crystallizes on cooling). With KI: bright yellow precipitate of PbI2.

notes: PbCl2 is unusual in being more soluble in hot water than cold. The yellow PbI2 precipitate is a distinctive confirmatory test.

name: Iron(II) Ion (Fe2+)

wet_test.procedure: Add aqueous Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH) dropwise. Alternatively, add Potassium Ferricyanide (K3Fe(CN)6) solution.
wet_test.result: With NaOH: a green precipitate of Fe(OH)2 forms, which turns brown on exposure to air. With K3Fe(CN)6: a dark blue precipitate (Turnbull's blue) forms.

notes: The air oxidation of the green Fe(OH)2 precipitate to brown Fe(OH)3 is a key distinguishing feature from Fe3+.

name: Magnesium Ion (Mg2+)

wet_test.procedure: Add aqueous Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH) dropwise, then add excess NaOH.
wet_test.result: A white precipitate of Mg(OH)2 forms and is insoluble in excess NaOH.

notes: Distinguishes from Zn2+ and Al3+ (both amphoteric — their precipitates dissolve in excess NaOH). Mg(OH)2 is not amphoteric.

name: Aluminum Ion (Al3+)

wet_test.procedure: Add aqueous Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH) dropwise, then add excess NaOH.
wet_test.result: A white gelatinous precipitate forms initially, which dissolves in excess NaOH.

notes: Amphoteric, with identical NaOH behavior to Zn2+. Distinguished by: (1) flame test — Al gives no color; (2) adding excess NH3 — Al precipitate does NOT dissolve, but Zn precipitate does.

name: Silver Ion (Ag+)

wet_test.procedure: Add dilute Hydrochloric Acid (HCl) to the solution.
wet_test.result: A white curdy precipitate of Silver Chloride (AgCl) forms, which dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia.

notes: AgCl darkens on exposure to light due to photodecomposition to silver metal. This is the basis of traditional photography.

name: Potassium Ion (K+)

dry_test.procedure: Flame Test: Dip a nichrome wire in concentrated HCl, then in the salt, and hold in a roaring Bunsen flame. View through cobalt blue glass.
dry_test.result: Produces a lilac / pale violet flame (visible through cobalt blue glass).

notes: The cobalt blue glass filter is essential to mask any sodium contamination, which would otherwise overpower the faint lilac flame.
